newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa commits to equitable 25 pct tax ceiling.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa commits to equitable 25 pct tax ceiling.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel on Monday reaffirmed his commitment to a global tax ceiling equal to 25 percent of GDP but said tax reform would have to ensure a fair and equitable distribution of the load.

Manuel told parliament the overall tax rate would have to fall slightly to the 25 percent level targeted in his June 1996, macreconomic framework for growth, employment and redistribution, known as GEAR.

"Within that, key questions relate to the optimisation of revenue collection, taking into account issues such as our history of tax morality, poor collection and disparities of wealth and income levels," he said.
Manuel said the Katz Commission on tax reform would publish final reports this year including a holisitic review of the tax system by November.

"Work is currently under way which should give us an indication of our total tax base...but total transformation must go beyond that into providing the type of tax structure that fits into our overall objective of collecting the budgeted level of tax revenue in a manner that ensures fairness and equity," he said.
Manuel said a policy white paper on budget reform, including plans for the formal implementation of a medium-term expenditure framework (MTEF), would be published for comment this year.
"The MTEF will be tabled with the 1998/99 budget and will consist of three-year rolling budgets for each department and province.
"This will provide cabinet with a framework within which to evaluate a menu of policy options and therefore competing bids (for funds)," he said.
Manuel said medium-term financial planning would provide a measure of certainty for planners, eliminate funding bottlenecks and reduce the tendency towards year-end budget rollovers.
Amongst his department's legislative plans was a proposal that would go before parliament this year to give legislators the right to amend so-called money bills.
At present parliament can debate, but not amend legislation dealing directly with annual revenue and expenditure.
